Q: How to detect wake word or if any word was said A:

My work around is to make the command that runs Pocketsphinx into a subprocess and pipe output into my python script.

import subprocess
p = subprocess.Popen("pocketsphinx_continuous -inmic yes", stdout=subprocess.PIPE, bufsize=1, shell=True)
for line in iter(p.stdout.readline, b''):
    print line.upper(),
p.stdout.close()
p.wait()

The line that says "print line.upper()" looks like in terminal

INFO: continuous.c(275): Ready...
INFO: continuous.c(261): Listening...
A lot of various pieces of information
THE WORDS YOU SAID

This works in real time!

Q: Changing the auto-generated task names in dynamic tasks A:

You do that this way (it also works with dynamic DAGs):

@task()
def foo():
    pass

with DAG(
    'test_foo',
    start_date=days_ago(1),
    schedule_interval=None,
) as dag:
    for name in ["a", "b", "c"]:
        foo.override(task_id=name)()

You can read more here: https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/tutorial/taskflow.html#reusing-decorated-tasks

Q: Is there anyway to recognize just one word without using speech to text api in python A:

I think what you want to do is wake word detection or keyword spotting. In wake word detection, the goal is to trigger the output when a specified word is heard in input.

There are several good libraries to do this. For example check these ones:

https://github.com/Picovoice/porcupine (it requires access key from their website)

https://github.com/MycroftAI/mycroft-precise (It looks like its free)

Q: Is /[\s\S]/ the same as saying /.|\n/ in regex A:

Take a look at the MDN's Regular Expressions JS reference:

/.|\n/

  • Wildcard: . - Matches any character except line terminators, unless the s flag is set.
  • Disjunction: | - Matches any of a set of alternatives separated by the | character.
  • \n - Character escape representing U+000A (LINE FEED)

Line terminators are defined by the MDN's Lexical Grammar JS Reference:

Only the following Unicode code points are treated as line terminators in ECMAScript, other line breaking characters are treated as white space (for example, Next Line, NEL, U+0085 is considered as white space).

Code point Name Abbreviation Description Escape sequence
U+000A Line Feed <LF> New line character in UNIX systems. \n
U+000D Carriage Return <CR> New line character in Commodore and early Mac systems. \r
U+2028 Line Separator <LS> Wikipedia
U+2029 Paragraph Separator <PS> Wikipedia

These four symbols are excluded by ., and only <LF> falls back in \n.

/[\s\S]/

  • Character class: [...] - Matches any character in a set of characters. When the v flag is enabled, it can also be used to match finite-length strings.
  • \s - Character class escape representing whitespace characters
  • \S - Character class escape representing non-white-space characters

The MDN's Regex Character Class Escape JS Reference says:

\s Matches any whitespace or line terminator character.

So it accepts the four chars defined in the above table.

If you really want to use the wildcard, you must use the s flag to match line terminators.

Q: MS Access re-uses already established ODBC connections, disregarding differing connection parameters A:

Microsoft Access can reuse an existing ODBC connection, and this can make it appear as though Access is ignoring different connection parameters.

This is particularly common when multiple linked tables use the same DSN/driver/server identity but specify different connection attributes. Access/ACE may pool or reuse the underlying ODBC connection rather than establishing a completely independent connection for each linked table.

What’s happening

For example, suppose you have two linked tables:

  • Connection A → Server=DB1;Database=Sales;User=UserA

  • Connection B → Server=DB1;Database=Sales;User=UserB

You might expect two independent connections. Instead, Access/ACE can recognize that the connection is compatible with an existing connection and reuse it. As a result, settings that you expected to be connection-specific—particularly authentication/session properties—may effectively come from the already-open connection.

This is related to ODBC connection pooling, but there is an important distinction: Access/ACE itself can also maintain/reuse connections for linked-table operations, so simply disabling the driver's ODBC connection pooling doesn't necessarily eliminate all reuse.

If you're troubleshooting this

A few things are worth testing:

  1. Use different DSNs even if they ultimately point to the same server/database.

  2. Put the differing parameters into the DSN itself, rather than relying on attributes appended to the connection string.

  3. Close all recordsets/forms/queries using the linked tables before changing credentials.

  4. Completely close the Access database and reopen it to ensure existing ACE connections are gone.

  5. If using a DSN-less connection, make the connection strings sufficiently distinct rather than assuming every supplied attribute will cause a new physical connection.

  6. Check the driver's ODBC connection pooling configuration separately from Access's connection management.

If you tell me which ODBC driver/database you're using (e.g. SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL) and show the two connection strings you're using, I can explain exactly why Access is reusing the connection and how to force the desired behavior.
